claim: Pupil size modulated in synchrony with changes in front-surface color, dilating when black.
source: Pupil size modulated in synchrony with the changes in front-surface color (dilating when black).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: The magnitude of pupillary modulation was larger for human participants with higher Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ).
source: The magnitude of pupillary modulation was larger for human participants with higher Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ), consistent with a local perceptual style, with attention focused on the front surface.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2B (r = 0.45, p<0.001).

claim: The modulation with surface color and its correlation with AQ was equally strong when participants passively viewed the stimulus.
source: The modulation with surface color, and its correlation with AQ, was equally strong when participants passively viewed the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from the no-report experiment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No other indicator, including involuntary pursuit eye movements, covaried with AQ.
source: No other indicator, including involuntary pursuit eye movements, covaried with AQ.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing no correlation between gaze-velocity differences and AQ (Figure 2D: r = 0.10, p=0.485).

claim: Bistable illusory motion is not necessary for the pupil modulation effect or its dependence on AQ.
source: These results reinforce our previous report with a similar bistable stimulus (Turi, Burr, & Binda, 2018), and go on to show that bistable illusory motion is not necessary for the effect, or its dependence on AQ.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the finding that the effect persists with stereo-disambiguated stimuli.

claim: Typical development brings about a gradual shift from local to global focus.
source: Typical development brings about a gradual shift from local to global focus (see Goodenough, 1976; Kimchi, 2015; Wagemans et al., 2012 for reviews).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Individuals with autism show biases toward local processing.
source: However, individuals differ in their tendency to focus locally or globally, and there is growing evidence that individuals with autism show biases toward local processing (for meta-analysis, see Van der Hallen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: Autistic individuals outperform neurotypicals in tasks where fine-grained visual features must be abstracted from their global context, such as the embedded figure task.
source: Autistic individuals outperform neurotypicals in tasks where fine-grained visual features must be abstracted from their global context, such as the embedded figure task (Shah and Frith, 1983) or the Navon figures (Plaisted et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Many local-global processing tasks are sensitive to task instructions and may be affected by cognitive strategy.
source: However, it has been pointed out that many of these are sensitive to task instructions, and may also be affected by cognitive strategy (see Baisa et al., 2019; Horlin et al., 2016 for reviews).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: There is a pressing need for objective and quantitative indices of the local-global preference.
source: Therefore, there is a pressing need for objective and quantitative indices of the local-global preference.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of existing measures discussed in the previous sentence.

claim: In the previous study (Turi et al., 2018), a pupillometry-based index revealed a strong relationship between local-global processing styles and autistic-like traits.
source: In our previous study (Turi et al., 2018), we introduced a pupillometry-based index that revealed a strong relationship between local-global processing styles and autistic-like traits, assessed in neurotypical adults by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) questionnaire (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: In the previous study, observers viewed a classic bistable motion illusion comprising transparent fields of black and white dots moving in opposite directions.
source: Observers viewed a classic bistable motion illusion (Andersen and Bradley, 1998; Treue et al., 1991), comprising transparent fields of black and white dots moving in opposite directions, giving the impression of a cylinder rotating about its vertical axis, with the direction of rotation and the color of the front surface changing periodically.
evidence: This describes the stimulus used in the previous study, with citations to the original illusion.

claim: In the previous study, pupil size modulated in synchrony with perceptual reports, dilating when the front surface was black and constricting when white.
source: Pupil size modulated in synchrony with perceptual reports, dilating when the front surface was black, constricting when white.
evidence: This describes findings from the previous study (Turi et al., 2018).

claim: In the previous study, the magnitude of pupillary modulation varied with AQ, stronger for participants with higher AQ scores.
source: Importantly, the magnitude of pupillary modulation varied with AQ, stronger for participants with higher AQ scores, consistent with attention being focused on the front surface (local style).
evidence: This describes findings from the previous study (Turi et al., 2018).

claim: Participants with lower AQ scores showed smaller or no pupil modulations, consistent with attention being distributed over the front and rear surface of the cylinder at all times.
source: Participants with lower AQ scores showed smaller or no pupil modulations, consistent with attention being distributed over the front and rear surface of the cylinder at all times (global style).
evidence: This describes findings from the previous study (Turi et al., 2018).

claim: The neural dynamics underlying bistable phenomena are complex and only partially understood.
source: Firstly, the neural dynamics underlying these phenomena are complex and only partially understood (Brascamp et al., 2018), and it is unclear whether any of these perceptual or decisional factors drive the pupil modulations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Susceptibility to visual illusions correlates with autistic traits.
source: In addition, susceptibility to visual illusions also correlates with autistic traits (Chouinard et al., 2016; Happé, 1996; Mitchell et al., 2010; Pellicano and Burr, 2012), making it difficult to judge whether the differences in pupil modulation reflect differences in susceptibility to illusions rather than differences in perceptual style.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing this correlation.

claim: Subjective reports of perceptual alternations may be unreliable and difficult to obtain from some participants, particularly young children and clinical groups.
source: Finally, although the pupillometric measurements are objective, their analyses relied on the subjective reports of perceptual alternations, which may be unreliable and difficult to obtain from some participants, particularly young children and clinical groups.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about the challenges of obtaining subjective reports from certain populations.

claim: The authors adapted the technique so it does not rely on illusory reversals by disambiguating the 3D rotation of the cylinder with binocular disparity cues.
source: To address these concerns, we adapted the technique so it does not rely on illusory reversals, by disambiguating the 3D rotation of the cylinder with binocular disparity cues.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study.

claim: Observers viewed the display through a stereoscope, and stereo-depth was periodically swapped to bring either the black or white dots to the foreground.
source: Observers viewed the display through a stereoscope, and stereo-depth was periodically swapped to bring either the black or white dots to the foreground, which also changed the direction of rotation of the cylinder.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and procedure.

claim: The modified stimulus allowed analysis of changes in pupil size based on objective changes of stereo-depth rather than perceptual reports.
source: This modified stimulus allowed us to analyze changes in pupil size based on objective changes of stereo-depth, rather than perceptual reports.
evidence: This describes the advantage of the modified methodology.

claim: The modified stimulus allowed elimination of the need for participants to report their perception.
source: It also allowed us to eliminate completely the need for participants to report their perception, simply observing the alternating stimulus for a period of time.
evidence: This describes the advantage of the modified methodology.

claim: Fifty-three participants reported the changes in rotation direction during 60 s trials while pupil size and eye movements were monitored.
source: Fifty-three participants reported the changes in rotation direction during 60 s trials, while we monitored pupil size and eye movements (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Pupil size modulates with the brightness of the foreground, dilating when black and constricting when white.
source: This figure has the same format as Figure 1B in Turi et al., 2018, but while Turi et al., 2018 aligned the traces to the perceptual reports of a bistable stimulus, here they are aligned to physical changes in the stimulus, ignoring perceptual reports. We define zero as the end of the stereo-switch, which lasted 1.2 s. This procedural difference leads to differences in the overall shapes of the pupil timecourses, but the basic result is the same: pupil size modulates with the brightness of the foreground, dilating when black (blue traces of Figure 2A) and constricting when white (red traces).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in pupil size for the two directions of rotation begins to emerge after the depth swap is complete and remains for several seconds.
source: The black trace at the top of Figure 2A shows the difference in pupil size for the two directions of rotation, which begins to emerge after the depth swap is complete, and remains for several seconds.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pupil-size modulations are consistent with attention being focused on the front surface.
source: The pupil-size modulations are consistent with attention being focused on the front surface, as a relative pupil dilation or constriction is expected from attending to black or white, respectively (Binda et al., 2013; Mathôt et al., 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to studies showing pupil responses to attended brightness.

claim: Pupil-size modulations cannot be explained by changes in luminance, as it was constant during the whole experiment.
source: It is important to reiterate that here, as in Turi et al., 2018, pupil-size modulations cannot be explained by changes in luminance, as it was constant during the whole experiment, nor by changes in the luminance distribution over space, as the white and black dots formed two overlapping transparent surfaces.
evidence: This is stated as a control for alternative explanations of the pupil modulation.

claim: There were large interindividual differences in the amplitude of pupil-size modulations.
source: As in our previous study, there were large interindividual differences in the amplitude of pupil-size modulations, and again a large portion of the variance could be accounted for by the participants' AQ score.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The correlation between pupil modulation and AQ is positive, strong, and highly significant (r = 0.45, p<0.001, lgBF = 1.49).
source: Figure 2B plots the pupil modulation (difference in size for the two directions of motion) against AQ of each participant. The correlation is positive, strong, and highly significant (r = 0.45, p<0.001, base-10 logarithm of the Bayes Factor [lgBF] = 1.49), showing that the magnitude of the effect increases with AQ.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The magnitude of the pupil-size modulation effect increases with AQ.
source: The correlation is positive, strong, and highly significant (r = 0.45, p<0.001, base-10 logarithm of the Bayes Factor [lgBF] = 1.49), showing that the magnitude of the effect increases with AQ.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The magnitude of pupil-size modulation depends on the tendency to focus attention locally on the front surface or globally across both surfaces.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the magnitude of pupil-size modulation depends on the tendency to focus attention locally on the front surface (hence driven by surface color) or globally across both surfaces, and that these two strategies correspond well to the local and global perceptual styles associated with high and low autistic traits (Grinter et al., 2009; Happé and Frith, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to studies on perceptual styles in autism.

claim: Local and global attentional strategies correspond to the local and global perceptual styles associated with high and low autistic traits.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the magnitude of pupil-size modulation depends on the tendency to focus attention locally on the front surface (hence driven by surface color) or globally across both surfaces, and that these two strategies correspond well to the local and global perceptual styles associated with high and low autistic traits (Grinter et al., 2009; Happé and Frith, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on perceptual styles in autism.

claim: The illusory bistable nature of the stimulus in Turi et al., 2018 is not the primary force driving the modulations in pupil size.
source: Firstly, it implies that the illusory bistable nature of the stimulus in Turi et al., 2018 is not the primary force driving the modulations in pupil size (although it might play a secondary role, accounting for the much higher correlation coefficient observed in our previous study).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that the effect persists with stereo-disambiguated stimuli.

claim: Modulation of pupil size is not yoked to processes of perceptual decision and report.
source: Secondly, it suggests that modulation of pupil size is not yoked to processes of perceptual decision and report, given that it can be driven by information about the physical stimulus only (see also below).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that the effect persists when analyzing data synchronized to physical stimulus changes rather than perceptual reports.

claim: The overall pupil responsivity could not account for the correlation between pupil modulation and AQ.
source: As in our previous study, we verified that the overall pupil responsivity could not account for this effect, as the mean pupil response (the size of the overall pupil dilation in the 1–2 s window following the depth swap) was reliably uncorrelated to AQ scores (r = −0.12, p=0.39, lgBF = −0.81, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, left column).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perceptual performance was uncorrelated with AQ (r = 0.12, p=0.42, lgBF = −0.82).
source: Moreover, in line with the previous findings, perceptual performance was uncorrelated with AQ (r = 0.12, p=0.42, lgBF = −0.82; here we measured performance as accuracy, by cross-correlating perceptual reports with stimulus stereo-depth timecourses and taking the peak of the function).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical values provided.

claim: Most participants made periodic horizontal eye movements with a slow phase in the direction of the cylinder rotation and a fast return phase.
source: Although participants were instructed to maintain fixation continuously on a salient mark throughout the experiment, most made periodic horizontal eye movements, with a slow phase in the direction of the cylinder rotation and a fast return phase (antagonistic OKN behavior, typical of transparent motion displays [Niemann et al., 1994]: see Figure 1B for example).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, with a citation to a study on OKN behavior.

claim: The slow phases of gaze shifts were generally consistent with the direction of the foreground dots.
source: We analyzed the slow phases of these gaze shifts and found them generally consistent with the direction of the foreground dots (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gaze-velocity differences were not correlated with AQ scores (r = 0.10, p=0.485, lgBF = −0.86).
source: Although there was interindividual variability in this behavior (with some tracking the rear dots), this was not correlated with AQ scores (Figure 2D), with Bayes factor indicating that the lack of correlation was significant (r = 0.10, p=0.485, lgBF = −0.86).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Factoring out gaze-velocity differences did not attenuate the correlation between pupil-size modulations and AQ.
source: Consistently, factoring out gaze-velocity differences did not attenuate the correlation between pupil-size modulations and AQ (partial correlation: r = 0.44, p<0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical values provided.

claim: When pupil-size data were re-analyzed synchronized to perceptual switches rather than stereo-depth swaps, the difference between pupil-size traces still correlated significantly with AQ (r = 0.39, p<0.01, lgBF = 0.72).
source: First, we re-analyzed our pupil-size data synchronized to the perceptual switches, rather than the stereo-depth swaps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The difference between pupil-size traces still correlated significantly with AQ (r = 0.39, p<0.01, lgBF = 0.72), indicating that our pupil-size modulation index is robust and relatively independent of the method used for parsing traces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compare the left and the middle columns).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pupil-size modulation index is robust and relatively independent of the method used for parsing traces.
source: The difference between pupil-size traces still correlated significantly with AQ (r = 0.39, p<0.01, lgBF = 0.72), indicating that our pupil-size modulation index is robust and relatively independent of the method used for parsing traces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compare the left and the middle columns).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that the correlation persists across different analysis methods.

claim: In the no-report experiment, the timecourse of the pupil-size difference was very similar to the main experiment.
source: The detailed form of the phase-locked timecourses of pupil size (Figure 3A, individual blue and red traces) differs from those in Figure 2, probably reflecting the lack of a pupil-dilation component linked to making and reporting perceptual decisions (Einhäuser et al., 2008). However, the timecourse of the pupil-size difference was very similar across experiments (compare the top black trace in Figures 2A and 3A), and its magnitude was clearly correlated with AQ score (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown by comparing Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: In the no-report experiment, the magnitude of pupil-size difference was clearly correlated with AQ score.
source: However, the timecourse of the pupil-size difference was very similar across experiments (compare the top black trace in Figures 2A and 3A), and its magnitude was clearly correlated with AQ score (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Correlation coefficients for the pupil-size difference and other parameters were similar between the main experiment and the no-report experiment.
source: Correlation coefficients for the pupil-size difference and the other parameters were similar to the main experiment, where participants made active reports (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compare leftmost and rightmost columns).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlation between pupil-size difference and AQ scores did not differ across experiments (Fisher test: F = 0.3, p=0.76).
source: The correlation between pupil-size difference and AQ scores did not differ across experiments (Fisher test: F = 0.3, p=0.76).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical values provided.

claim: There are multiple independent components of the pupil-size modulations related to observation of the complex stimulus.
source: These results support the hypothesis that there are multiple independent components of the pupil-size modulations related to observation of our complex stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of results across different experimental conditions and analysis methods.

claim: There is a transient dilation related to the key-press action, which was not correlated with AQ (r = –0.15, p=0.29, lgBF = –0.72).
source: There is a transient dilation related to the key-press action (absent in the no-report experiment), best seen when time-locking pupil traces to the perceptual switches as in Figure 2—figure supplement 1: this component was not correlated with AQ (r = –0.15, p=0.29, lgBF = –0.72).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a transient constriction related to the perceptual change, which did not correlate with AQ (r = –0.32, p=0.13, lgBF = –0.31).
source: There was also a transient constriction related to the perceptual change, isolated in the no-report experiment in Figure 3, which again did not correlate with AQ (r = –0.32, p=0.13, lgBF = –0.31).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a relatively sustained pupil-size modulation measured by the difference between traces for the two possible 3D layouts of the stimulus, which was similarly observed in both experiments.
source: Finally, there was the relatively sustained pupil-size modulation, measured by the difference between traces for the two possible 3D layouts of the stimulus, and similarly observed in the two experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: AQ scores were specifically correlated with the sustained pupil-size modulation component (r = 0.38 or larger, p<0.05 and lgBF >0.6 in all cases), irrespective of whether perceptual reports were used for analysis or dispensed with altogether.
source: AQ scores were specifically correlated with this component (r = 0.38 or larger, p<0.05 and lgBF >0.6 in all cases), irrespective of whether perceptual reports were used for analysis or dispensed with altogether (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for a summary of the AQ-correlation analyses).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pupil-size difference has the highest test-retest reliability among all measured parameters.
source: Although all parameters are significantly correlated across experiments, pupil-size difference has the highest test-retest reliability, in spite of having the lowest split-half reliability.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The disattenuated correlation between experiments for pupil-size difference is particularly high (r = 0.93).
source: Indeed the disattenuated correlation between experiments (right column of Figure 4), computed with the Spearman-Brown formula (Spearman, 1910), is particularly high (r = 0.93).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pupil-size modulations are noisy but consistent over time, suggesting they are driven by stable individual differences.
source: This indicates that pupil-size modulations are noisy but consistent over time, suggesting that they are driven by stable individual differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the high test-retest reliability despite low split-half reliability.

claim: Other indices (besides pupil-size difference), although more consistent within any experimental session, are far less consistent over time, possibly affected by the participants' time-varying state or the task requirements.
source: In contrast, the other indices, although more consistent within any experimental session, are far less consistent over time, possibly affected by the participants' time-varying state, or the task requirements.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of reliability measures shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neither the complex neural dynamics underlying bistable perception nor the act of reporting a perceptual decision is critical for inducing a modulation in pupil size.
source: These results show that neither the complex neural dynamics underlying bistable perception (Brascamp et al., 2018) nor the act of reporting a perceptual decision is critical for inducing a modulation in pupil size.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that the effect persists with stereo-disambiguated stimuli and in the no-report condition.

claim: The reproducibility of pupil-size differences across the two experiments is testimony to its stability over time, which may be as high as r = 0.93 when the noise in each individual measurement is taken into account.
source: The reproducibility of pupil-size differences across our two experiments is testimony to its stability over time (which may be as high as r = 0.93 when the noise in each individual measurement is taken into account).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the disattenuated correlation shown in Figure 4.

claim: One component of pupil-size modulation is a transient pupil dilation time-locked to the reporting of a perceptual decision, previously associated with increased arousal and norepinephrine release.
source: One is a transient pupil dilation, time-locked to the reporting of a perceptual decision, and previously associated with increased arousal and norepinephrine release (Einhäuser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on pupil dilation and arousal.

claim: Another component is a transient pupil constriction time-locked to the occurrence of a stimulus change, which may be interpreted as an 'onset' or 'grating response' associated with visual cortical activity.
source: Another is a transient pupil constriction, time-locked to the occurrence of a stimulus change that may be interpreted as an 'onset' or 'grating response' (Barbur et al., 1992), associated with visual cortical activity (Sahraie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on pupil responses to visual stimuli.

claim: The sustained pupil-size difference depending on the 3D layout of the stimulus is compatible with the effect of attending to bright against dark, mediated by a cortical circuit.
source: Finally, there is a more sustained pupil-size difference depending on the 3D layout of the stimulus; this is compatible with the effect of attending to bright against dark (Binda et al., 2013; Mathôt et al., 2013), mediated by a cortical circuit (Binda and Gamlin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on attention-related pupil responses.

claim: Only the stimulus-dependent modulation of pupil size correlated significantly with participants' AQ.
source: Only the third of these, the stimulus-dependent modulation of pupil size, correlated significantly with participants' AQ.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The pupil-size difference is not easily explained as a pupillary near response.
source: Note that the pupil-size difference is not easily explained as a pupillary near response (the pupil constriction that accompanies near vision, Marg and Morgan, 1949).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to a study on the near response.

claim: For the near response to influence the results, participants (especially those with higher AQ) would need to follow a particular color continuously, whether in front or behind.
source: For this to influence the results, participants (especially those with higher AQ) would need to follow a particular color continuously, whether in front or behind.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be required for the near response to explain the results.

claim: The gaze-velocity data shows that most participants (irrespectively of their AQ) tended to track the horizontal motion of the front surface.
source: However, the gaze-velocity data shows that most participants (irrespectively of their AQ) tended to track the horizontal motion of the front surface (Figures 2D and 3D), suggesting there was no stimulus-driven change in vergence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 3D.

claim: OKN-like gaze behavior could in principle have been informative of how participants distributed attention.
source: This OKN-like behavior (Niemann et al., 1994) could in principle have been informative of how participants distributed attention (Mestre and Masson, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on OKN and attention.

claim: Gaze shifts are at least partially under voluntary control and were explicitly discouraged by asking participants to maintain fixation on a central mark.
source: However, unlike pupil-size changes, gaze shifts are at least partially under voluntary control and were explicitly discouraged by asking participants to maintain fixation on a central mark.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is based on knowledge about voluntary control of eye movements.

claim: The tendency or ability to follow fixation instructions depends on a number of factors (e.g. motivation), which may be unrelated to AQ and might have masked any underlying correlation with AQ scores.
source: The tendency or ability to follow the instructions depends on a number of factors (e.g. motivation), which may be unrelated to AQ and might have masked any underlying correlation with AQ scores.
evidence: This is speculation about why gaze behavior might not correlate with AQ.

claim: Differences in gaze behavior could not have generated differences in pupil-size modulations, as these were not necessarily stronger in participants who tended to track the foreground dots more systematically.
source: On the other hand, the finding that gaze behavior is unrelated to AQ also indicates that differences in gaze behavior could not have generated differences in pupil-size modulations, as these were not necessarily stronger in participants who tended to track the foreground dots more systematically.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between gaze behavior and AQ.

claim: Pupillometry provides an index of local-global preference which is reliable and stable over time.
source: In summary, besides replicating (twice) the association between pupil-size modulations and autistic traits, the two experiments reported here confirm that pupillometry provides an index of local-global preference, which is reliable and stable over time, as may be expected for a parameter driven by genuine individual differences.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Data from the no-report experiment may be considered proof of principle that pupil measurements are informative even in a situation that requires minimal cooperation of the participants.
source: In addition, data from the no-report experiment may be considered proof of principle that pupil measurements are informative even in a situation that requires minimal cooperation of the participants, which could pave the way for its implementation in a clinical sample with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and implication of the no-report experiment findings.

claim: Experimental procedures were approved by the regional ethics committee and are in accordance with the declaration of Helsinki.
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the regional ethics committee (Comitato Etico Pediatrico Regionale—Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Meyer—Firenze [FI]) and are in accordance with the declaration of Helsinki; participants gave their written informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval and compliance.

claim: Fifty-three neurotypical adults (41 women; age [mean ± SD]: 25.6 ± 3.3 years) volunteered to participate in the study.
source: Fifty-three neurotypical adults (41 women; age [mean ± SD]: 25.6 ± 3.3 years) volunteered to participate in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no diagnosed neurological condition.
source: All reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no diagnosed neurological condition.
evidence: This describes inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Sample size was set based on the previous study (aimed for N = 50 and recruited three more to prevent data losses).
source: Sample size was set based on the previous study (we aimed for N = 50 and recruited three more to prevent data losses, which fortunately did not occur).
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size determination.

claim: All neurotypical adult participants filled out the validated Italian version of the 50-item Autism-Spectrum Quotient questionnaire.
source: All neurotypical adult participants filled out the validated Italian version of the 50-item Autism-Spectrum Quotient questionnaire (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Ruta et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the assessment tool used, with citations to the original and Italian validation.

claim: AQ responses are made on a 4-point Likert scale: 'strongly agree,' 'slightly agree,' 'slightly disagree,' and 'strongly disagree.'
source: Responses are made on a 4-point Likert scale: 'strongly agree,' 'slightly agree,' 'slightly disagree,' and 'strongly disagree.'
evidence: This describes the response format of the AQ questionnaire.

claim: AQ items were scored as one when the participant's response was characteristic of ASD (slightly or strongly), 0 otherwise.
source: Items were scored as described in the original paper (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001): one when the participant's response was characteristic of ASD (slightly or strongly), 0 otherwise.
evidence: This describes the scoring method with a citation to the original paper.

claim: Total AQ scores ranged between 0 and 50, with higher scores indicating higher autistic traits.
source: Total scores ranged between 0 and 50, with higher scores indicating higher autistic traits.
evidence: This describes the range and interpretation of AQ scores.

claim: There were no significant gender effects on AQ scores (two-sample t-test: t(51) = 0.31, p=0.76, lgBF = −0.48).
source: There were no significant gender effects on either AQ scores (two-sample t-test: t(51) = 0.31, p=0.76, lgBF = −0.48) or on our pupil measurements (pupil difference in the main experiment: t(51) = 1.38, p=0.17, lgBF = −0.18).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical values provided.

claim: There were no significant gender effects on pupil measurements (pupil difference in the main experiment: t(51) = 1.38, p=0.17, lgBF = −0.18).
source: There were no significant gender effects on either AQ scores (two-sample t-test: t(51) = 0.31, p=0.76, lgBF = −0.48) or on our pupil measurements (pupil difference in the main experiment: t(51) = 1.38, p=0.17, lgBF = −0.18).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical values provided.

claim: As the male gender was under-represented in the sample, the results on gender effects should be considered with caution.
source: However, as the male gender was under-represented in our sample, these results should be considered with caution.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of gender effects given the sample composition.
